utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Is there anything to be raised before we begin today? Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. First of all, our team wants to welcome back Mr. Sladojevic who is married now and we are happy to have him back with us. Mr. President, the next witness, KDZ601, is proposed as a witness under 92 ter, and it's our request that you require his testimony be given viva voce. The material that the Prosecution proposes to use for the 92 ter statement is an investigative interview, a transcript of an investigative interview that was done with the witness in 2005. And we believe that this is not a proper document which should serve as a 92 ter statement which is the equivalent of direct examination, has the same weight as direct examination. This was an exploratory essentially first interview by an investigator with this witness some six years ago. We believe that Rule 92 ter doesn't apply to this kind of interview because the text of 92 ter says that a Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement, which this is not, this is a transcript of an oral interview, or a transcript of evidence given by a witness in proceedings before the Tribunal, which this is also not. It's not a transcript of proceedings before the Tribunal in terms of testimony before in another trial. And we think that this is particularly -- should be applied in this case because this interview is almost incoherent. The witness skips around from topic to topic. He talks about collecting information from people, since the initial meeting with OTP. That's at page 10. He offers to get names and forward to the investigator, that's at page 12. He talks about comments made at a burial by unknown people at page 18. He talks about things he learned in the middle of last year, which would have been 2004, some 12 years after the events, on page 19. And then on page 23, he says this is my assumption, when he's talking about something. So I don't think that this is a kind of document the Chamber should accept as something in lieu of direct testimony because most of this would never have been allowed if the witness were giving evidence before a Court and I would ask that the Chamber ask the witness -- if you're in doubt, ask the witness whether or not he would give the same -- whether he would say these same things if examined which is part of Rule 92 ter(A)(3). Because in our interview with him yesterday, he said that while what he said was the truth or was accurate, that it was not in a format or in a form in which he was very clear. So for all of those reasons we would ask that the Chamber hear this witness viva voce. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to this witness, I would submit that any of the arguments that Mr. Robinson has raised are matters which can be dealt with by Dr. Karadzic during the course of his cross-examination. Something -- if something is offered by the witness, as Mr. Robinson refers to, which might be without an explanation for its basis, that's also -- that's a matter which goes to weight rather than a basis on which to convert a witness to be heard live. When I hear this and when I was first informed of this argument, I went back to the transcript of evidence, wondering if I'd been completely misguided in my earlier assessment, and I found nothing that would warrant such a dramatic measure. Rather, I found matters which could be -- benefit from an amplification which is what we propose to do during the evidence in-chief today. So, Your Honours -- and indeed, Mr. Robinson has already indicated that during the course of the interview last night, the witness stated that he found the transcript to be an accurate transcript. So I would submit there is absolutely no basis to convert the witness to anything other than what he is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether you can help us as to the -- in regards to the legal issue, whether written statement would include an investigator's interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me point out briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can make reference to something, either jurisprudence or decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, yes, thank you. We would have been in a better position to do so if this matter had been raised with us earlier when we were notified that the matter would be raised. This legal issue was not referenced in any way whatsoever. So we would of course have gone to the books to address that issue had it been raised. Now, dealing with it on my feet at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking because I remember having dealt with similar issues in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can find the jurisprudence and hopefully we could find it quickly, but, as I say, that was the problem and we are not immediately prepared with the citations at hand. However, I would say that it should be clear from the text of 92 ter that it is not -- that the formality comes in the attestation by the witness in open court saying, This written document here, that's what I'd say to you. There is no need to repeat it. I've read it. It's accurate. You can rely on it. That's the point. The previous formalities are not the issue. So in -- and if it was, then you could have the admission of that document without the need for the witness in court. So these are two quite separate matters. I think on the face of 92 ter, this argument is specious, but unfortunately because we were not notified that this particular argument would be made, although there was ample opportunity to do that, I can't cite the particular jurisprudence for you at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add something, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe we have dealt with this issue once before and I'm not exactly sure which witness it was. It may have been KDZ-555, and I think that you rejected our argument and then when it -- had to hear the witness and decided that he should testify viva voce for other reasons. That's my recollection of that. But for Mr. Tieger's benefit, it was on Saturday that I notified him that we would be objecting and we would be asking that there be viva voce testimony, and he scolded me to the Chamber for including argument in my e-mail. So I think it's a little bit inconsistent to be complaining that I didn't raise the issue and make the argument in advance when, in fact, I did give them quite a bit of notice that we were raising this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I really do need to clarify that. As I responded to Mr. Robinson at that time, his point was the one that -- he's made two points, the one that Ms. Edgerton referred to. And that is based on his e-mail she went back to the document to see whether the substance of the document, which was exactly -- which was what Mr. Robinson said he objected to, was problematic. And we -- Ms. Edgerton looked at it. I looked at it. I responded to Mr. Robinson's e-mail on that basis saying that his factual assertions about what was or wasn't in the document were inaccurate based on our review of the document. There was no suggestion that he was going to make this legal argument and that's what I'm responding to now. So it's true he said he was going to raise an objection but it wasn't this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have found where that sort of thing has been dealt with previously, and it's with respect to a witness who had no protective measures, Dragan Vidovic. In that case, a transcript of an audio recording of an interview with the OTP was admitted as a 92 ter statement for that witness, and that was P3191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And at the time, was an objection raised in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload P3191? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a reminder, and I'm grateful to Mr. Robinson for this acknowledgement, as he noted it was raised in another context; in other words, this very argument by Mr. Robinson was raised before the Court, rejected by the Court, although that particular witness was heard viva voce for other reasons. So it's been admitted without objection and it's been rejected by the Court when the objection was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise to consider this matter for about a quarter of an hour. --- Break taken at 9.17 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the ruling of the Chamber: The Chamber is of the view that the transcript of an interview conducted by the OTP investigator is included in the written statement in the context of Rule 92 ter. The Chamber wishes specifically to refer to the decision made in the Popovic et al. case which was issued 31st of May, 2007, on the motion to convert viva voce witnesses to Rule 92 ter witnesses. The Popovic Chamber in that decision stated that the main purpose of Rule 92 ter is to foster the efficient and expeditious conduct of trial proceedings in accordance with the rights of the accused, and therefore, there is no reason to limit the scope of Rule 92 ter to a specific means of documenting evidence, and in general, the requirement of a written statement should be considered as fulfilled when the witness's words are documented and preserved. The Chamber further stated as to the concern about the authenticity and veracity of transcript of audio-recorded interviews, that the Chamber is satisfied by Rule 92 ter, which sets out a sufficient framework of safeguards by requiring that the witness will attest in court to the accuracy of his or her written statement and be available for cross-examination. The Chamber further stated that although a transcript of an audio-recorded interview includes the words of the interviewers, this Trial Chamber is composed of professional judges with the experience and ability to discern the contents of evidence and give it the appropriate weight. Finally, the Chamber also stated that the accused will not be prejudiced as a result of the admission of a transcript of an audio-recorded interview as a written statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and that excluding the transcript of an audio-recorded interview from the scope of Rule 92 ter would be contrary to the underlying rationale of that rule. This Chamber adopts the reasoning taken by the Popovic Chamber. Further, although in the context of Rule 66(A)(ii), the Chamber notes the Appeals Chamber decision where it defined the meaning of "witness statement" in relation to Rule 66(A)(ii), where it stated the account -- where it stated that witness statement is to be interpreted as the account of a person's knowledge of a crime, which is recorded through due procedure in the course of an investigation into the crime. The Chamber is of the view that that Appeals Chamber's definition is also consistent with the Chamber's ruling. Further, we note the previous practice in which the interview transcript has been admitted in this proceeding. I would like to end with the remarks to Mr. Robinson that in the future, if it relates to the matter of principle, the objection should be raised at the first moment available. Unless there is any other matters to be raised, we will bring in the witness. We should go into private session? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to lift the curtain. Sir, before you begin your testimony, I wanted to say a few words to you first. You will be referred to in the proceedings as KDZ-601. In this regard, you will be testifying with the benefit of pseudonym, which is KDZ-601, as I said to you, and image and voice distortion. This means that there will be no reference to your real name or information which might reveal your identity to the public or media. Also, the audiovisual record of your testimony, which is broadcast to the public, will have a distorted image, and distorted voice to ensure that your identity is protected. I think we can show the image to the witness, image of the witness. This will be how you'll be seen to the public. And the transcript, while available to the public, will always refer to your pseudonym. Do you understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Miss Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 65 ter 90275, the pseudonym sheet, brought up, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you understand me in your own language? Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in a few moments, you'll see displayed on the computer monitor in front of you a sheet of paper with your pseudonym number and your name on it. Is your name accurately set out there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that as the first exhibit under seal in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3298, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, back in 2005, you were interviewed by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor from this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was that interview audio-recorded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: It was audio-recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And yesterday, in preparation for testifying here this morning, did you read a transcript in your own language of that recording?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you find it to be accurate, as far as you're able to remember?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: That was it, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I was to ask you all the same questions today that you were asked at that time, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I'd give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then could I tender 65 ter 22641, the transcript of the audio recording we just referred to, as the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we already made our objection noted and you rejected it so nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. For the reasons indicated earlier on, we will admit it. We reject the objection of the -- from the Defence and we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3299 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a brief summary of the written evidence that's just been filed. The witness was a member of the Bosnian Serb police forces serving and active in and around Bosnian Serb-held Sarajevo in the early part of 1992, in the months after the outbreak of war. His evidence refers to two detention facilities in the Sarajevo municipalities, Kula and the gymnasium as Pale. He talks about the presence and actions of paramilitaries in areas of the western peripheries of the city of Sarajevo, making reference to Branislav Gavrilovic, the White Eagles, volunteers from Belgrade and Arkan's men, as well as Oljaca's Chetnik group. The witness talks about the transfer of prisoners between Hadzici, Lukavica and Kula, as well as between Kula and the gymnasium in Pale, and also the exchange of detainees at Vrbanja Bridge. Detainees at the Kula prison were brought there by the VRS, police and paramilitary groups. The witness visited the scene of the bus massacre in Ahatovici, Scheduled Incident B.12.2 in relation to this indictment, and gives evidence related to that incident. That's the summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I'd like to ask you some additional questions generally related to that evidence. My first question is regarding the duties of the officers at the Kula police station. Did that include manning the front lines?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: That was compulsory. There was an order from the public security station of Ilidza and of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know who served as chief of the public security station of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The chief of the public security station of Ilidza was Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Mr. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know what areas officers from the Kula station -- what areas of the front line officers of the Kula station served at?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Several places. I'm going to refer to all of them. First of all, Dobrinja. Now, I'm not sure whether it's 1, 2, 3 or 4. I don't know what the separation there was at the time. Then the Jewish Cemetery. And the area of Mojmilo, Ozrenska, Zagorska Streets, in the combat area, in the area where the separation was too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the Jewish Cemetery and Ozrenska an Zagorska Street also within the territorial jurisdiction of Ilidza municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Only Dobrinja fell under the territorial jurisdiction of the municipality of Ilidza, the rest was the municipality of Novo Sarajevo and part of the Old Town, Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In these other areas which fell within Novo Sarajevo and the Old Town, Stari Grad, do you know under whose operational command officers from the Kula station were when they served at those locations of the front line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: In co-ordination with the special unit of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded that special unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Mr. Milenko Karisik, commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did local civilian authorities ever request support from units that were part of the Kula police station?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: There were requests from the Crisis Staff, and the chief of the public security station of Novo Sarajevo would refuse that as unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "requests from the Crisis Staff," do you mean to refer to any Crisis Staff in particular?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Kasindol, the Crisis Staff that was stationed in Kasindol.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to keep on the subject of the duties of the officers that were part of the Kula police station, the guards at Kula were also for a period part of the Kula station, were they not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Belonged to the Ministry of Justice. However, in terms of work assignments, they were deployed at the Kula police station because there was an agreement between the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, and Momcilo Mandic, because it was impossible, as far as I know, to have the Ministry of Justice open a gyro account of his own and pay salaries. However, it was noted that they were guards of the KP Dom Butmir, the correctional facility of Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday, in preparing for your testimony, we had a second look at a sketch of the Kula compound you had drawn some years ago, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And yesterday, did you make some additional markings on that sketch?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I made some additional markings, and I placed numbers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at that sketch, please. It's 65 ter 23243A, and it shouldn't be broadcast because of the name that appears on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this the same sketch you annotated yesterday, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain a couple of additional markings or the markings you made yesterday to us. Do we need to enlarge that image for you or can you see it okay?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in a bit more, if possible? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is the main entrance to the Kula compound marked on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What's it marked with?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: A red arrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you lift this sketch up a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to make it upside down?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And zoom further.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the red arrow, then, identifying the main entrance?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that the red arrow with the number 4 beside it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What's marked -- what did you mean to designate with the marking of the number 5?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Number 5 indicates the area where a policeman was on duty, controlling the main entrance. This is an area where the public security premises were located, as well as those belonging to the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there any tanks in the compound at Kula?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, there were two tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are they marked here on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: They are marked with number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did they remain at those locations or did they move?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: At night-time, they would move about, or in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where would they go to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: They would go to the intersection not far from the KP Dom, and on a couple of occasions, they moved in the direction of the road leading to the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Whose tanks were they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: They were tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army. As the JNA withdrew, they came to belong to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on this sketch I see a number of crosses marked with the number 7. Does that designate anything?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The markings with the number 7 indicate the locations where members of the special units of the Army of Yugoslavia were billeted as well as the crews operating the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember how long the special units of the Army of Yugoslavia remained billeted there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: They stayed there until the hand over of the airport in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said in your written evidence that civilians were brought into Kula by the military, the police and paramilitary forces, and that's at page 13. I wonder whether you saw if these JNA forces you've just referred to did the same.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. Especially the special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember how this special unit, the members of the special unit, were dressed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As any other elite special unit, its members had a special sort of uniform, and they had infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These infantry weapons that they had and the special sort of uniform, could you describe them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I will try to recall them as best I can. These were camouflage uniforms with flak jackets over them, protective helmets and protective collar. The weapons were infantry, small arms, the calibres ranging from 9 to 12 millimetres. Some of the weapons they had I saw for the first time there and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did those uniforms and equipment and weapons compare with, for example, the equipment and arms and material of the members of the police station at Kula?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The difference was in the quality and colour. What they had was far more modern and lethal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how did you know that they belonged to the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The cars that they used bore the insignia of the JNA, or rather of that special unit. I can't really remember what it looked like. They were under the command of a professional officer wearing a special uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can just go back to this sketch for a moment, if you could please move it a little bit so we could see the bottom part of the page displayed, there is a rectangle on this sketch with a small X on it marked with the number 2, Mr. Witness. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there anything located in this building?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: It was a small structure built of very strong material. It had two small rooms where interrogations took place of the individuals who were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you know who conducted those interrogations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I know that authorised members of the state security of the Ministry of the Interior carried out these interrogations, as did members of the military security of the JNA, and the operatives of the crime police of the public security station of Novi Grad Kula, as well as members of the various centres and the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one last question for everyone's benefit, probably about how to understand this sketch. When you looked at the sketch yesterday, did you see it had been preserved on two separate sheets of paper?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if -- how, then, should we understand how the two pieces of paper relate to one another?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before you do, perhaps we could call up 65 ter 23243, which is the unannotated version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I wonder if we might be able to display the two pieces of paper side by side, and, please, not for broadcast. That's not it yet. Still not. 23243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 3 of four pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean Page 3 of that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need to turn around one of the pages. I leave it in your hands because I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we'll all know soon, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, does the way these two pages are laid out now accurately reflect the layout of the Kula complex, if you -- as you remember it? Or do they need to be rearranged?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I find it difficult to gather what this sketch is. I think that this sketch, and correct me if I'm wrong, indicates an area where for sometime before my arrival there, shells landed from the positions of the BH Army at Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. That's what you explained in your statement. And, Mr. Witness, if we took the image that's depicted on the left-hand side of the page and shifted it over to the right and then took the image that's on the right-hand side of the page and shifted it over, would that more accurately depict the layout of the compound of Kula, as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if we just reverse the order of these. And then the image on the right-hand side of the page, if we could turn it upside down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As displayed, Mr. Witness, does this layout represent an accurate rendering of the compound at Kula, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how so not? And it's just in terms of how these two pages relate to one another, how they should be displayed so the Chamber and all of us understand. Do we need to rearrange the two pages again?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Would you kindly give me the other sketch, which indicates part of the fence of the KP Dom compound and the police station. I think that the other sketch indicates accurately the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then I think we -- I think the witness might be asking for 23243, page 1 to be displayed on the right-hand side. Is this what you were looking for, Mr. Witness? I just want to know if these two sketches as laid out are how the Judges should understand the layout of the compound.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: No, no. The sketch on the left-hand side needs to be replaced with the other sketch where you can see the fence or the edge of the compound of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I'll leave that until I can understand a little bit better what the witness is referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But in the meantime, I'd like to tender 23243A, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you were with the witness when he marked the numbers, new numbers, and put his signature --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- you could have asked him to put his pseudonym instead of his real name so that we can admit it publicly. Just bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3300, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think, though, Your Honours, as I look back, with respect, I might have made the decision I did because his initials appear on the original version as well. So I was constrained. But moving at speed again, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I misunderstood that his initials were made recently but it was made a long time ago, in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We could remove that from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you confirmed a short while ago that paramilitary forces were involved in bringing civilians into Kula, and I'd like to know whether any units, and you named some of them at page 14 of your statement, were more involved in this than others.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: From what I was able to observe in my line of duty, I stated what I did in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were any paramilitary units more involved in bringing prisoners to Kula than others?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Units of the JNA, in that period of time, and less so some of the other self-organised and self-proclaimed units, because there weren't many of them in that period, as well as the Territorial Defence of the Vojkovici area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was the Chetnik Oljaca group involved in bringing prisoners to Kula?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, in co-ordination with Territorial Defence of Vojkovici, the battalion there, and as far as I know, to a lesser extent, independently.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did have you occasion to see the commander of the group who, I assume from your description, was named Oljaca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I did. Because he would drop by the Kula police station and the public security station, as well as by the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember how he would be dressed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I remember it clearly. It was for the first time then that I saw black uniforms, woollen uniforms, and the cockade on the peaked cap that their commander wore. I was told that he was a major by rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know where he came from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I was told that he came from the area of Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know in what army he held that rank of major?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I think it was a rank belonging to that Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know in what area or what municipality he acted in?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, in the area of Kotorac, Ilidza, and solely the areas in the direction of Ahatovici and Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The prisoners that he and members of this group would bring to Kula, do you know -- did those prisoners that were brought to Kula, that you've referred to, come from those locations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: From what I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicities of those prisoners you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I assume they were Serbs. I could tell that by their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you -- how did you come to know their names?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I heard it from my work colleagues who were in touch with the KP Dom. There were several names of those who were members of that Chetnik unit who, for having committed certain infractions during combat activities, had been sanctioned by their own commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I understand you learned the ethnicities of prisoners from some of your colleagues, and you also learned that there were members of that unit who had been sanctioned for certain infractions. Did you also -- did you learn that from your colleagues as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, were the prisoners that this group brought to Kula exclusively Serb, or did -- were there other ethnicities as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: There were several ethnicities. All the groups and all the participants in combat activities, or, as they call it in practice, combing activities, would, as a result of that, bring in men, all the men from an area who would be interrogated and thereafter sent to other locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where would the Serbs who were brought in and interrogated be sent? What would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they were sent to the Lukavica Barracks. Some of those who had previously been members of the reserve police force downtown or in the periphery were deployed to man the Kula police station, which was understaffed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What would happen to the non-Serbs who were brought in and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: From what I know, in that period of time, exchanges were arranged, but quite a lot of crime was committed as well. This came out later on when information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that some of the members of this unit were sanctioned by their own commander for infractions they had committed. What kind of -- do you know what kind of infractions those were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Based on what I was told, it involved drinking and individuals who failed to perform the obligations and tasks they were given by their commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did that group, Oljaca, remain in place in the area as long as you did?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What makes you think so?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Had they been removed or had they left, I would have probably found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where were they based?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The information that I have indicates that they were stationed between the Kotorac and Vojkovici neighbourhoods in houses of people who had been moved out, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In which municipality does Kotorac -- do the areas of Kotorac and Vojkovici fall?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will move on then to another area.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you aware what units -- first of all, are you aware of the location of the settlement of Ahatovici in the western periphery of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Right now, yes, but during the war, I wasn't aware of that settlement, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know that the settlement was attacked by Serb forces in late May and the first days of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you learn --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene. In the transcript, the witness did not say "yes," but he said "cuo sam," "I heard." And that's different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How did you answer, Mr. Witness? Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I heard, but you could also confirm it with a yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you learn what units took part in this attack on Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Among other things, the group of Chetniks, reinforced with the battalion and also members of the police forces from that station area, the Ilidza Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The group of Chetniks, referring to a group in particular?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: It's the group that we were discussing, the Oljaca group of Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And members of police forces from what station area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the public security station Ilidza, that comprised a number of reserve forces police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: From conversations with people who would come to Kula, and from the operatives who were conducting these talks with the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What people who would come to Kula? From conversations with what people who would come to Kula?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The operatives of the Novi Grad security station that was based in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. You talked about two sources of information on which you based your answer. The first was conversations with people who would come to Kula, and the second was the operatives who were conducting talks with these people. When you referred to the operatives of the Novi Grad security station that was based in Kula, are those the operatives who were conducting talks with people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Basically yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The operatives who were conducting talks with captured people?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think the answer at page 26 calls for a redaction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to go back to the first part of your answer, you said you also learned this, who had taken part in the attack, from conversations with people who would come to Kula. What people were they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Members of the public security station, the station in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to move on, but also still on the subject of events in Ahatovici, in your written evidence, you referred to the shooting of a bus load of prisoners from Ahatovici, saying that Gavrilovic, Branislav Gavrilovic, and his units were the group that shot up the bus. And that's at pages 37 to 39 and 42 to 43. So I wonder how you know that it was Gavrilovic and his unit who did this. What's the basis of your information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, there is a misunderstanding here. I mentioned Gavrilovic in the context of Kasindolska Street. I would need to look at that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I will try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pages 37 through to 39, and 42 and 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness does that, I wonder what time you were contemplating for the breaks today given that we had a late start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Depends upon how much longer you would need to conclude your in chief examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At least ten minutes, probably not more than 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll break after your examination-in-chief is over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So could you just tell us how -- what makes you believe, or how you know that Gavrilovic was responsible for shooting the bus load of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: By going to the Vogosca police station, to the chief of the station's office, where a number of operatives were present, there was talk about that event, and one of those present said that that was that group of Gavrilovic. I said that there was a misunderstanding because I viewed that case with the bus, that incident, separately where some people were hurt. Separately from the Ahatovici operation. But it is true that I did hear that in that police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to move on, you referred in your evidence to 10 to 12 buses of civilians coming from Hadzici to Kula one night and you said that they were taken to Lukavica. Do you remember approximately the date that that took place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but it is true that one twilight, just as it was getting dark, those buses did appear at the entrance of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember if the date was -- if this happened before or after the airport was handed over?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I cannot really say either way, but thinking, just like that, it's possible that this perhaps happened before the hand over, but I don't know how they could have arrived unless they used a round-about route of some 250 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With the type of escort that you outlined in your written evidence, military police and police, would such a route have been easy to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I think that that route would be exhausting and risky, and I'm not sure if the buses could tackle the macadam curves in the road, especially in Centar municipality, Nahorevo, Crepoljsko and Stari Grad neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where did they arrive from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: They said that it was the Hadzici area towards Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you learn the ethnicity of the people on the bus?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. They were Muslims, Bosniaks, Muslims at that time. That's what was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your written evidence, you referred to the cleansing of Kotorac by military troops, and that's at page 5. Which military troops were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The forces or the troops of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: The operation was conducted by a professional JNA officer, Major Sladoje or Sladoja, I'm not sure. That's his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When did this take place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I think it was in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why do you think it was in June?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I allow for the possibility that it was late May, early June. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, finally, you referred in your evidence to two members of the Srpska Narodna Garda in black uniforms who introduced themselves as the deputy and assistant of Arkan coming to Kula. Do you remember when this was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: In the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take a break now for half an hour and we will resume at 10 to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We forgot to deal with associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Exactly why I'm on my feet, Your Honour. I've only got one outstanding associated exhibit, 23244, that I'd like to move in, please, Your Honour. That was an exhibit, actually, that in our notification we had requested leave to add as well. But it is referred to in the witness's written evidence at pages 61 to 64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted, but what about 65 ter 23243?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the annotated version of that, so in addition to the markings he put on the original version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's sufficient to cover. The annotated version is only two pages, if I'm correct, if my memory is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think so, too, Your Honour. And I can't remember, actually, as I stand on my feet whether I had actually tendered that document as well, and my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Annotated version was admitted as Exhibit 3300.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and we had the discussion about it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in terms of completeness, we can admit this one as an associated exhibit, if there is no opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 23243, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, of course, 23244 doesn't have the same restrictions at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 23243 will be Exhibit P3301 under seal, and 65 ter 23244 will be Exhibit P3302.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, you will be further asked by the accused, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Mr. Karadzic, in light of the fact that we -- he's a protected witness, please formulate your questions so as not to reveal the identity of the witness. And, sir, whenever you find that your answer may reveal the identity of yourself, please don't hesitate to let us know to go into private session. Do you understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, your Excellencies. Good day to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, good day.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Thank you. Good day to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As always, Excellencies, I'm going to do everything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. For planning purposes, we will break at 1.00 for an hour. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm just saying that as always I will do everything to take the witness's circumstances into account and I would kindly also ask for the OTP, and I will also respect that, when we approach anything sensitive, that we would ask for a private session but I see that Mr. Tieger is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Only for a scheduling matter. I wonder if under the circumstances -- I think we had an inquiry from VW whether they should be advised that the next witness will not be expected to testify today and can be brought back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be the case. I don't think we will be able to finish the cross-examination of this witness today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, first of all, thank you for meeting with the Defence via videolink yesterday, and I hope that that will help us to clarify things that need clarifying, and once again, I would like to thank you for that. I would like to ask you a little bit about the pre-war period, that is also something that you touch upon in your statement. You were not a member of any party and you were not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: No, I was not. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, and I have to ask myself, to make breaks between question and answer so that the interpreters could keep up. And if you follow the transcript, then you will see when they are finished.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was a general inter-party level of the coalition party, the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ about the distribution of posts from the Presidency down encompassing all the important posts in the state organs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, one way to find when you should start your answer is take a look at the transcript, and when it stops, it's time when the interpretation has been completed. Please take it into account. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that immediately after the elections, there were quite considerable tensions because the SDA did not stick to the agreement, namely it did not rush to appoint the Serbian cadre even though the Muslim cadre was already in place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I remember that period, and I attended numerous talks amongst my colleagues who belonged to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serbian Democratic Party left its cadre policy in the police forces to professionals who, at those higher senior official levels, were not members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I am aware that what you are asserting is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know at the time, or did you find out later, and I believe that you probably did know this at the time, that Serb cadres were illegally monitored, those in the police and those in the political posts, by Muslim cadres or personnel who had taken the eavesdropping equipment and placed it at the disposal of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I am aware of the eavesdropping, and also monitoring some of the Serb cadres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that, already in the spring of 1991, the secret arming of the Muslim people started, through Slovenia and Croatia and through alleged humanitarian organisations, and that this arming was assisted by high officials of the MUP who were ethnic Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: To be quite honest, in order to have the truth proven, I learned about that from the media. Later on, as I did the work I did in the Ministry of the Interior, I became convinced by way of written dispatches and other information coming from the field.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I would suggest moving into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this question should be redacted altogether; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible, could you rephrase?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't need to do that. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, therefore, that obviously there were separations very early on along ethnic lines within the MUP, from top to bottom but especially at the top? Also that this resulted in the marginalisation of Serb personnel and their removal from positions where they could have insight into the secret arming and preparations for the creation of a BH Army within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I remember that period of time. And I'm not very happy to comment on it, but I will try, as briefly as possible. I personally did not have such problems, but there were public security stations and police stations where there were serious problems. Among others, I would like to mention the second station within Sarajevo centre and it has to do with the commander, the "komandir." People who worked there for a long time and who were professionals, tried to keep this professionalism and this homogeneous nature of the work involved. However, people who came from the ranks of general citizens took some top positions and, believe me, I say this as a human being and a professional, it was very hard for professionals to carry out their duties. That is what I have to say by way of an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that the positions that belonged to the Serb people were not taken by individuals who had never been in the police force before; whereas the SDA brought you Mirsad Srebrenikovic and other people like that who were actually priests by vocation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I could agree with your statement, and there were these cases. Things like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember -- or, actually, did you know that on 31st of March, a decision was made on the establishment of the Patriotic League, and on the 30th of April the Patriotic league was formed, all of this in 1991, or did you find out about that later?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Good friends of mine who were ethnic Muslims told me about that

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on 10th or 11th of June 1991, at the Dom Milicije, a secret or semi-secret meeting was held, a large gathering, where the council of the SDA for the defence of Muslims was established and that the meeting was secured by policemen who were ethnic Muslims only?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I'm aware of that case, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If necessary, that can be redacted as well. Actually, that is why I dealt with this in closed session. Do you know that the president of that council was Mr. Izetbegovic, who, as president of the Presidency, was the president of the joint council for defence in the republic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I learned about that a month or two after the event actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any knowledge to the effect that the Green Berets, or rather, the Patriotic League, or rather, these groups -- actually, do you agree that they included a large number of criminals, like Juka Prazina and the like?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I knew about that. That is correct, that quite a few criminals were in these Green Berets. Later on, we had many problems with these persons as we carried out our regular duties, we in the public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the time considerably before the war, when they were taking over particular facilities; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: That kind of thing did happen. That is correct. And there were serious problems in student dormitories, at the hospital in Kosevo and so on. That is to say, facilities that were covered (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that, for example, they were checking who was coming and going to and from the Kosevo hospital considerably before the war started?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: It is correct that they carried out checks. We had serious problems when we intervened in that hospital of Kosevo, especially in the period of time when Mr. Ostojic was brought to the hospital, when he was wounded in the area of the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the minister of information in the joint government who was beaten up by metal bars; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for reminding me, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that what had been noticed was that prominent Serbs or Serbs who were disliked or most Serbs, especially officials in the police and former officers, pensioned/retired officers, had markings placed on their doors so that people would know that it's a Serb apartment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: That was something that happened - and citizens reported that, as did military personnel and other officials - primarily in the municipality of Centar in the neighbourhood of Ciglane where most of these high-ranking officers lived. Perhaps you had occasion to see a memo that I wrote to the Prosecutor's office or the Defence stating that my apartment had been marked as was the apartment of Professor Miskovic, a very well known professor at the Sarajevo University. I think that this hasn't been removed to this day from my door. It was carved in, the letter V, it was two centimetres long and one centimetre deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this alarming? Did that alarm persons who realised that their apartments had been marked?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: In conversations with people who reported on such occurrences, we felt that they were panic-stricken, that there was trepidation in their souls and that they were concerns about the safety of themselves and their families. I personally was not upset. I thought that this was an irresponsible group of people who were doing that, but later on what turned out to be the case was actually quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What turned out to be the case later? Was this efficient? Did this indicate to criminals where they could go in and do something?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it turned out to be the case in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that at some point in early 1990, or 1991, a film was broadcast which had been secretly filmed with the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, Spegelj, who gave the following instructions: You ring the bell. When they answer the door, you fire a bullet and move on. Was it not the case that coupled with this information, the markings placed on the doors proved to be terrifying?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I do recall that period of time and I do recall the broadcast. It was aired repeatedly on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was clear that Minister Ostojic had been beaten up by Muslim extremists and that a lot was done to cover up and suppress this information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: That was the information that the general public was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there was an increased number of reserve policemen and the tendency was to have more Muslim reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: There was an increase in the reserve police force as early as in October. Lists were drawn up based on percentages and calculations made on the basis of the senior officer cadre in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the SDA, in documents signed by Hasan Cengic, deployed members that were otherwise not part of the police force for training to Croatia in order to turn them into policemen one day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I did hear that information. Mr. Cengic resided in an area that

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: (redacted) who were of a moderate political stance told me this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of the negotiations concerning the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and did you know that they resulted in the signing of the Cutileiro agreement in March of 1992, whereby three constituent units would have existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the three peoples?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of it. I followed these events on television and in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that it envisaged a great deal of powers for these constituent units, such as education, health care, almost everything except for the foreign affairs and defence, and that, in among other things, a constituent unit would be entitled to its own police force?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. I do recall the negotiations and the contents of the various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in late March, in other words after the acceptance of the agreement, two MUPs were set up, or, rather, the Serb MUP was set up but the Muslim side was pretty undecided? They were considering the establishment of a joint Muslim-Croat MUP, but it had not yet been established by that time.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I do recall that period of time. I remember the negotiations, and I can only say that it was quite a difficult period for the professionals working within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in that period, it was quite unadvisable to deploy Serb policemen to chase down criminals in a Muslim neighbourhood, and vice versa? In other words, that there was ethnically based distrust within the police force?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I do recall that period. I remember official documents and working meetings where orders were given to take strict care of the ethnicity of a policeman before he or she is deployed to an area. I assure you that it was a very difficult thing to deal with for the policemen and it was highly unpracticable for the work on the ground. My apologies. There were even cases of citizens who sought police intervention, would even in some cases send away policemen from their yard even without knowing what their ethnicity was, even if they were of the same ethnic group. This affected the work of the police. The practice showed that citizens would seek intervention through individual chiefs of police stations rather than through the appropriate call in duty services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that these paramilitary and criminal gangs were -- felt quite safe in their own neighbourhoods? And do you agree that it would not have been wise to send a Serb policeman to Hrasnica or Stari Grad or perhaps dispatch Muslim policemen to Pofalici or some other Serb neighbourhood? Do you agree that criminals, in fact, could be quite resourceful on the basis of what the ethnicity of a policeman was and it affected police work? What I want to say is that in addition to the abusive policies in the MUP where they wanted to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I'm sorry to intervene. Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question? In particular, the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me simplify. Do you agree that the general distrust that existed, as well as information about abusive practices in the MUP with a view to establishing Armija, the Armija, was this the reason why Cutileiro was asked that under the agreement the policing powers should fall to individual constituent units?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a professional, you frowned upon this idea, did you not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, your superior told you at some point that you should refrain from coming to work for a while, for your personal safety and security. Did you see this suggestion as a well -meaning one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I did spend a great deal of time with that individual. We socialised a great deal. So I felt that it was a well-meaning comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that your Serb colleagues in areas where Serbs were the majority, advised their colleagues that they should not show up for work for a while until the situation calmed down? Was this not the sort of courteous relationship that existed among colleagues?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. There were such conversations taking place between individuals of the same ethnicity or different ethnicities, that one should side with one's own people and join the newly-established MUPs. Those were the conversations taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript does not reflect what you said about the newly established MUPs which had been agreed upon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was an answer to my next question, but let's clarify this. This sort of courtesy and amicable relations, was it not the reason why members of one ethnicity would advise members of another ethnicity not to come to work for a while, for their safety, just as your boss told you? This was not meant as a dismissal from work but simply lying low, if we can say so, for one's own safety.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you came to Vraca and were then dispatched to this other station, the name of which we will not mention. Is it accurate that you found that the station was quite -- had quite a shortage of men and equipment? We could call up 148 -- 1D4187. Unfortunately, Your Excellencies, we don't have a translation but it's mostly figures so I don't think there will be any problems. We -- the translation is pending. Please have a look. Is this a list of material and technical equipment available, and were their quantities sufficient? We can perhaps look at what there was a lack of, what was in short supply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the last page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Shall we go into private session, briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 4201 in e-court, please, 1D4201. And we can save on time. This is the testimony of Mr. Avlijas in the case of Lalovic and others at the Bosnia-Herzegovina court. Can we look at English page 14, let's say, and the Serbian page 19, since it's already in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put your question, simply? Why do you have to show and read out the transcript of other people's testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. That is accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that Slobodan Avlijas was a functionary of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. He was assistant minister of justice while I was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Lalovic, as the prison warden, and others were put on trial in Sarajevo at the Bosnia-Herzegovina court for events in the prison, and that they were acquitted in those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And since we have called up this document, can you please pay attention to what Avlijas said and whether this corresponds to what you knew, that this correction facility began to work sometime in July and although it was a misdemeanour detention unit before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: This was a lenient KP Dom where people were serving sentences of up to six months imprisonment and those who had been sentenced for lesser misdemeanours or traffic violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: And it's not true that it began to operate in July. When I came, I found those people there. The dom was operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that at the time it became a stricter prison than it was before, perhaps this is what he meant?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say. I have no idea what he was thinking, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that they did not have all the best conditions there, that there was a kitchen, that refugees were accommodated above the kitchen, that the Serbian population from Vojkovici and Krupac frequently moved and went to Kula or to the hospital, and is this something that corresponds to what you know and what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, I'm hearing this for the first time. I'm hearing this for the first time. I don't know where they could have been accommodated. I think I quite clearly showed the KP Dom facilities, those of the police, those of the justice ministry. I think that this had some kind of different objective. In the area above the kitchen, there were members of the special unit who were billeted there until they left, also the tank crews, and then a little bit farther down there were five rooms occupied by members of the police when they were off duty, which indicates that you cannot really accept this testimony, and this is something new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned this kitchen as a kind of popular kitchen where many who did not belong to the police station or the KP Dom also came to have food, and that it was really a kitchen for the people, for the poor, in the true sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, realistically speaking, all those who came, regardless if they were just passing through or if they were there on assignment or if they were employed there, they could use the kitchen. It was available to all those who wanted to use it, because the KP Dom had its own farm, and it had large food reserves because that was its main activity, food production. They had their own farming facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did they receive food regardless of their ethnic affiliation or their -- whatever group they belonged to? Could everybody have food regardless of their religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I can agree. I can say yes because it was not just the members of the KP Dom -- it was not just Serbs who were employed at the police station and the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that at the police station and among personnel of the KP Dom, there were those who were not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I want to say that there were employees in the police and in the KP Dom who were from mixed marriages, so you could not really say that they had a definite ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Excellencies, just checking whether your scheduling remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a break now for an hour and resume at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue and leave five minutes at the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that the line of separation between the Serb and Muslim or Muslim-Croat forces from the beginning until the end of the war was more or less the same, say between Gornji and Donji Kotorac and that is about 2- or 300 metres away from Kula?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And facing town, was the separation line in Dobrinja and that is, say, 3- or 400 metres away from the barracks and perhaps 500 or 600 metres away from Kula?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
