utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the front lines in Sarajevo often went along streets, in Dobrinja itself, even through a particular building, say the Serb army would be in one part of the building and the Muslim army would be in another part of the building?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: There were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to interpret for you -- actually, can you tell the Trial Chamber who Goran Macar was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I can expound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just say who he was and which position he held.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: In the old system, as we called this period, that was there before these unfortunate conflicts, he was the chief of the operations service in the public security station of Sarajevo. After the outbreak of the conflict, from the chief of the same service of the Serbian centre of Sarajevo to the head of the crime police in the headquarters of the police of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In these proceedings in Sarajevo that we mentioned -- I beg your pardon, this is the interview with the OTP, in case one of the participants wants to cast a glance, that is 1D4200; 52 and 53 are the English pages, and I'm not going to have this called up. It says that there was fighting, say, in Dobrinja and that sometimes 50 or 70 civilians would come to the barracks or to Kula from the front line and there were civilians of all ethnicities there, and then it says that Minister Stanisic ordered that as soon as conditions are created, that they should be sent back to their apartments. Is that your experience too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, you see, you will allow me to make a comment, and at the end I can make an assessment and you can draw your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your experience that during the fighting, from these buildings that were on the front line, were civilians brought from this front line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. Civilians were brought, large numbers, 50 to 100 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These civilians, were they of all ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, all ethnic backgrounds because at the front line, as practice showed, ethnicity could not be determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say in your statement, on page 17, lines 8 to 22, you say that during mop-up operations in built-up areas, persons were put up at the KP Dom. There were Muslims, Serbs, Croats, Roma and others. When you speak about mop-up, do you have in mind the military term, "Mop-up" of enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, you see I'm going to try to explain this, the term that I wished to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it helps you any, please take a look at your own statement. That is page 17. In Serbian, it is 16. Number 16. Page 16.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I found it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, let us see, when one speaks of mop-up in the context of a war, does one mean mopping up remaining enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, you see, perhaps I did not use the right term or perhaps it was not translated properly. I'm not sure. But this was a term that was used in the context of combat operations, at least in the area where I was. In some sense of the word, it can be accepted as "mop-up." I can try to explain because all the persons in that part of town were brought in, men and women. So I cannot define this specifically, this particular word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph, you say that operatives of the public security station were in charge of making assessments as to who should stay and who should be released; right? And there were Serbs there who had the same treatment, and they were transferred to Lukavica after interviews; Lukavica, is that because they were military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, they were military conscripts, and the army was manned by such persons. Some of them who had been engaged before the war were trained in the field of security and, therefore, they then manned police stations, depending on their place of residence. That was customary practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we are on the subject, was it easier to be a reservist in the police or was it easier to go to the front line? Was that a privilege, basically?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: People thought that it was a privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did it happen that you were cleansing your police of reservists who exhibited a lack of discipline or lack of professional training, and was that considered to be punishment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, I can agree there are written traces to that effect. Sometimes, say, there would be 10 or 12 reservists from a particular local commune, say Kasindol. They did not meet the appropriate criteria of being authorised officers, or, rather, being members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May the Chamber move into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what I'd like to see is whether the Serbs, Muslims, Croats and the Roma and all those you listed in this paragraph, if it is established that they are guilty, then there is one outcome. Otherwise, they are released. Whereas the Serbs, if they are under a military obligation, they are dispatched to the barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that I don't know what the standard practice was of operatives because that was part of their service. As far as the military conscripts are concerned, yes, I did have a standing order from my superiors that these individuals should be taken to Lukavica, being military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that this military obligation was in force only in respect of the Serbs and not the Muslims and the Croats and the rest?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 18 of English, and page 25 of Serbian, you say that the minister of the interior signed an order whereby all those detained and imprisoned should be treated in keeping with the Geneva Conventions and that this was -- this was placed on the announcement board in the police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not on page 18. Perhaps we could just double check the page in English that the answer that Dr. Karadzic is referring to appears on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Page 28. It's the 18th of April but the page is 28, lines 1 through 4. In Serbian, lines 11 through 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you can refer to your statement there.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. This was an order that was publicly announced, but the reference is not to prisoners but detained and captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. Detained and captured. So do you make this distinction between detainees, inmates and captives? Would somebody who is taken captive, somebody who is taken captive in combat, for instance? An inmate would be someone who is already serving a prison sentence; whereas a detainee would be someone who is under an investigation.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what happened in the process of interpretation there but the term I used was "detained," those detained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to call up 65 ter 18346 in e-court. Page 3 of the document. 65 ter 18346, page 3. It is quite possible that page 3 has not been translated, but can we please exhibit it because the witness will be able to identify it. Can we show it here? Apparently, the entire document has one page, which is translated, but we have the entire document. Can it be placed on the ELMO for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this 65 ter number Dr. Karadzic referred to is actually D01533, but now we are seeing - I'm not sure I understand - a fuller version of that document or other pages of that document or that's what Dr. Karadzic proposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were disclosed an entire batch of documents under this number. Perhaps subsequent modifications were made but we received these disclosures under that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's a totally separate document, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could just shove this document down on the screen a little bit so we can see the number on the top right-hand corner then we could see if we have some translations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ERN numbers are --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I can help everyone. This document that's on the ELMO was previously admitted as D1530, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you upload Exhibit D1530. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see the document? It is dated the 6th of September, but, despite that, is it consistent with what you know of the ministry's position? Perhaps go through the document rather than me read it all. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up in e-court 1D4192? Unfortunately we don't have the translation yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you done with the previous document which was shown under the number 18346? I wonder, if you put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. Since the document is already admitted, I have no further need of it. The witness said that he was familiar with the order and that he knew that there was a follow-up; other documents resulted from this one, orders as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that 18346 was marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Edgerton said that it had already been assigned a D number, that it's an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's been admitted, well, the first page only had the number of the entire batch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I checked the first one. 18346 has been marked for identification pending English translation. And having observed the evidence, it's time to admit it in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is my understanding correct? Is the document we discussed already admitted? It's got a D number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that has been already admitted but I was referring to the document you showed before that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we don't have the translation yet, but I'll summarise it. On the 17th of April, 1992, Mr. Stanisic sends a warning, and he says: In certain public security stations, cases were recorded of unlawful appropriation of moveables and immovables belonging to citizens, businesses and institutions which had been committed by members of our service. And they mean the police. It is further stated that the strictest of measures will be applied, including termination of employment, Prosecution, et cetera. Further down it says that certain individuals, who were involved in crime, did so sometimes in collusion with some of our members, and it goes on to say that she should be called to account before a court of law and that these assets should be seized from them. This was roughly at the time when you were transferred to the MUP. Is this consistent with your experience and knowledge about what the position of the ministry was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: At this time, I was on the first location. Not only were these municipalities, or, rather, public security stations indicated here involved in this, but, rather, the public security centre in Sarajevo, based on this letter, issued circulars informing check-points at certain locations. When I arrived at the location that I mentioned, I set up four or five check-points with a view to implementing this order, i.e., preventing the commission of crimes, including serious crimes, and ensuring unhindered movement of the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the stolen movable properties confiscated and stored in facilities? In any specific facilities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: In the police station where I worked, there was repository for such confiscated assets, in keeping with the relevant documents of the Ministry of the Interior. It was only the chief of the centre who could issue an authorisation to take any of the confiscated items out of the repository.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in the sixth line from the bottom, it is stated that the property should be given back to the rightful owners if they are known, and/or the properties should be kept in the repository until these proceedings come to an end.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Since the competent service did produce this, I guess this was the way things worked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1671, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask for assistance from the OTP, because I have a similar problem with the document from the batch 18346 bearing the ERN 0324-6103, so the ERN is 0324-6103. Has it been admitted as well? Perhaps we should place it on the ELMO so that it can be more easily identified. I do apologise, Excellencies. I received it as part of the same batch and it was a collective number, i.e., 18346 which covered several documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document that Dr. Karadzic has asked for to be put on the ELMO now, I don't know what 65 ter it had in the Defence list, but I'm told it's been admitted as D1525. Oh, and MFIed pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D1525 for a brief moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Witness, to look at an order issued by Mr. Mandic at the time he was in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To have the record completely clear, this was not part of the notified list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the ERN numbers, they are all in sequence, and that's the batch that we received. But very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this. At the time, Mr. Mandic was still in the Ministry of the Interior. This order was issued three days after Stanisic's order, and it bears similar contents. Can you tell us what this is about? Does it not say that there is an escalation of terrorism, violence and robberies in the territory under the control of our police, and that it is necessary to organise patrols in that area made up of the police force and reserve police force? That's under 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this order in the Ministry of the Interior at a much later date. I was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it not indicate assets that are found on an individual who cannot testify or certify to their provenance should be seized from them and stored in the police station?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is a document that was MFIed, can it now be admitted? We do have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, witness, that it's quite common among our people to blacken people generally, he's doing this, he's doing that, and that it's very hard to find one's way around these rumours? Is this something that happens in our neck of the woods?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- yes, that does happen but it's not just specific to our region. It's a common thing for all people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that there was some allegations that Stanisic, that Mandic, that Kovac, that they were doing something that was irregular in terms of property or any other way? Did you hear such rumours?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I did hear several times from policemen, from operatives, from people who had contacts with them. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D4195, please? I'm afraid that this translation is not there yet. So it's 1D4195.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that I formed a state commission to investigate this matter and that I appointed Vice-President Professor Nikola Koljevic to head that committee who was prone to believing that the rumours were true?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, I read the document at the Ministry of the Interior in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I ask you to read it for the transcript while we are waiting for the translation. Or you can just tell us -- actually, can you just briefly read this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He doesn't need to read it aloud to us. If he is reading it to himself, that's fine, but I'm waiting for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it evidence that Mr. Koljevic here informs that I appointed him and that he's asking all the data about the activities of Mandic, Stanisic and Kovac?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what we did at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall that it was his conclusion that there is no proof of any irregular activities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall the conclusions and the comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So not just financial but any other matters. Well do you know that these three people had quite tense relations with President Plavsic and Koljevic and then with Prime Minister Djeric, but they did their work honestly and they established that there was no proof that these rumours were correct and they excused these people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, I know that they had tense relations with the prime minister, Mr. Djeric. That's the only thing that I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you this: Being familiar with our political system --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today, I note you are extensively using untranslated documents. Please bear in mind the Chamber's warning. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1672, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, witness, sir, since you are familiar with our political and constitutional system, whether the president of the republic has any investigating body other than the regular police force.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: I know that in practice there should be a body that monitors the work, but at this time period that we are discussing, I'm not aware that there was any such commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the commission for the oversight of the work of state organs is part of the assembly body, and they are in charge of overseeing the work of the army, the police, and so on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the president himself cannot do anything else but form some kind of inquiry or commission and that the investigation is in the hands of the MUP and the justice system and not in the hands of the president?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm familiar with the matters, it's in the hands of the MUP and the justice system organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up D449 for a moment, please? We have a Serbian version as well. Could we have that on the other half of the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is from the 29th of November? It says 2002 up there -- no, no, we will see when the date is. It's on the other side. Is this a letter to the Prime Minister Djeric from the Ministry of the Interior? That this is what it states in the heading?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, it is addressed to Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then on the first page it talks about which crimes need to be investigated. Can we have the second page, please? And can I ask you, I'm going to read this underlined part: [As read] "We are working on the collection and documentation of war crimes, i.e., genocide, regardless of the perpetrators and their ethnicity." Witness, sir, your station, did it also take part in investigations of all crimes regardless of ethnicity and was anything ever covered up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: No. Not the police station, but the operative service of the police station, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They carried out investigations regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was, pursuant to the orders that we have seen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that when a criminal report is submitted and sent to the organs of the judicial system it's not possible to cover anything up any more, because it's then part of the regular procedure and that any point it would have to be resolved whenever the circumstances allow?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that's getting a little bit too far beyond the witness's field of knowledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness knows what a criminal report is, and when a criminal report is made, does that not, in a way, ensure that there is no cover-up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let us see whether the witness would be able to answer the question. Do you remember the question, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. When a criminal report is submitted to the authorised body, that is, the Ministry of Justice, the public security station centres and the ministry have a file. It's a so-called KU registry which records all the papers submitted to the authorised bodies. In regular proceedings, there is no possibility of any cover-up, except in the case of somebody abusing their post or position, and then deleting from the register and then write down instead some other indicia or number of a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to these duties of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now perhaps -- well, perhaps we can go to private session briefly. 1D4194, please. And I apologise in advance for the tardiness of the translation and I completely accept the criticism of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And be cautious when -- we go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, there was a question here about the commission or, actually, the documentation centre for the documenting of crimes against the Serbian people. Let's clarify something here. Were the powers for carrying out investigations of crimes committed on our territory something that remained under our police and judicial institutions? In our territory was this done by this documentation centre or was this something that was done by the police?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: At the seat of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, a body was formed or a commission, we could say, which dealt with the operative service of the criminal police which dealt with shedding light on the crimes committed in war -- on war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and as it says in this document, this was done regardless of the religious or ethnic background of the perpetrators; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I have a comment there. To be honest and professional, there weren't that many representatives of other ethnic or religious groups. It mostly focused on crimes against Serbs and this register also shows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that something existed which was outside of the police, outside of the MUP? It was the centre for documenting crimes against the Serbian people, headed by a writer Miroslav Toholj. There was no criminologist, lawyer or judge who was part of that body. It was an author, a writer, who documented things that the escaping Serbs brought back from the federation.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P1096, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that one ought to distinguish between the centre for documentations and investigating bodies?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-601
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript reads: [In English] There were not many [Interpretation] The witness said there were somewhat fewer of those. There were fewer investigations. Can we now have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will continue next week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we will rise soon for today and continue next week. I'm sorry not to be able to conclude your evidence this week, but that happens in the course of trial. Before we rise, I will give a ruling, oral ruling, with respect to the accused's 58th motion for finding of disclosure violation and for sanctions. Witness KDZ-052 which was filed on 6 September 2011. The Chamber has considered the arguments of the accused and the Prosecution's written response and finds that Prosecution violated its obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii) by only disclosing the transcript of the testimony of KDZ-052 on 5th of September, 2011, even though the testimony in question was given in October 2010. Having reviewed the 19 pages of testimony and considering the submission of the parties, the Chamber finds that the accused will have sufficient time to consider this newly disclosed document and incorporate it, if necessary, into his cross-examination of KDZ-052. Given the length and content of the new material, the Chamber is not convinced that the accused has been prejudiced by this late disclosure, but observes that it once again reflects poorly on the Prosecution's disclosure practices that such a statement was not disclosed sooner. In these circumstances, the requested exclusion of KDZ-052's testimony is denied. Mr. Witness, we will continue on Tuesday morning at 9.00. While we are adjourning, you are not supposed to discuss about your evidence with anybody else. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before we rise, if I could just call to your attention, we received during the course of the day the estimate for the cross-examination of the next witness, Mirzet Karabeg, which was three hours. I hope it was a typographical error -- and it was really eight hours because I just note that he testified in his direct examination for 7 and a half hours during the Brdjanin case, all of which is being incorporated into his 92 ter transcript. So I was hoping maybe the Chamber could revisit that if, in fact, we were only allowed three hours because it makes it very difficult when we have less than what the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was tendered is a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. It's a transcript from the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And he was cross-examined there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was cross-examined, but basically on the individual responsibility of those accused primarily. But he was examined in chief for 7 and a half hours approximately, cross-examined for about five and a half hours, and we feel that the allocation of three hours -- that Dr. Karadzic is way below what he would need, and if the witness had testified live, he would be testifying for 7 and a half hours to give that same information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider the matter. And as we close, the Chamber wishes to express its congratulations on Mr. Sladojevic's having tied the knot. And everybody have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: May I add, Mr. Sladojevic, that I wish you a happy and holy wedlock and pure and unadulterated marital bliss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
